claim: Shigella causes approximately 270 million yearly cases of shigellosis.
source: Shigella is a genus of enteric bacterial pathogens that causes ~270 million yearly cases of shigellosis, with ~200,000 of these resulting in death (Khalil et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately 200,000 cases of shigellosis result in death yearly.
source: Shigella is a genus of enteric bacterial pathogens that causes ~270 million yearly cases of shigellosis, with ~200,000 of these resulting in death (Khalil et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2018.

claim: Shigellosis manifests as an acute inflammatory colitis resulting in abdominal cramping, fever, and in severe cases, bloody diarrhea (dysentery).
source: Shigellosis manifests as an acute inflammatory colitis resulting in abdominal cramping, fever, and in severe cases, bloody diarrhea (dysentery) (Kotloff et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kotloff et al., 2018.

claim: Bacterial invasion of the colonic intestinal epithelium and subsequent dissemination between adjacent intestinal epithelial cells is believed to drive inflammation and disease in shigellosis.
source: Bacterial invasion of the colonic intestinal epithelium and subsequent dissemination between adjacent intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) is believed to drive inflammation and disease.
evidence: The claim is presented as an established belief in the field.

claim: Shigella pathogenesis is mediated by a virulence plasmid which encodes a type three secretion system (T3SS) and more than 30 virulence factors or effectors.
source: Shigella pathogenesis is mediated by a virulence plasmid which encodes a type three secretion system (T3SS) and more than 30 virulence factors or effectors (Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019; Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019 and Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008.

claim: The T3SS injects effectors into the host cell to facilitate bacterial invasion, escape into the cytosol, and disarmament of the host innate immune response.
source: The T3SS injects effectors into the host cell to facilitate bacterial invasion, escape into the cytosol, and disarmament of the host innate immune response to make the cytosol a hospitable niche for replicating Shigella (Ashida et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashida et al., 2015.

claim: The virulence plasmid encodes IcsA, a bacterial surface protein that facilitates cytosolic actin-based motility and is essential for bacterial spread to neighboring IECs.
source: The virulence plasmid also encodes IcsA, a bacterial surface protein that facilitates cytosolic actin-based motility and is essential for bacterial spread to neighboring IECs (Bernardini et al., 1989; Goldberg and Theriot, 1995; Mattock and Blocker, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernardini et al., 1989; Goldberg and Theriot, 1995; Mattock and Blocker, 2017.

claim: Programmed cell death eliminates the intracellular pathogen niche.
source: Programmed cell death eliminates the intracellular pathogen niche, maintains epithelial barrier integrity, promotes clearance of damaged cells, and enhances presentation of foreign antigens to cells of the adaptive immune system (Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017.

claim: Programmed cell death maintains epithelial barrier integrity.
source: Programmed cell death eliminates the intracellular pathogen niche, maintains epithelial barrier integrity, promotes clearance of damaged cells, and enhances presentation of foreign antigens to cells of the adaptive immune system (Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017.

claim: Programmed cell death promotes clearance of damaged cells.
source: Programmed cell death eliminates the intracellular pathogen niche, maintains epithelial barrier integrity, promotes clearance of damaged cells, and enhances presentation of foreign antigens to cells of the adaptive immune system (Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017.

claim: Programmed cell death enhances presentation of foreign antigens to cells of the adaptive immune system.
source: Programmed cell death eliminates the intracellular pathogen niche, maintains epithelial barrier integrity, promotes clearance of damaged cells, and enhances presentation of foreign antigens to cells of the adaptive immune system (Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deets et al., 2021; Doran et al., 2020; Jorgensen et al., 2017; Koch and Nusrat, 2012; Yatim et al., 2017.

claim: Cell death of IECs is accompanied by a unique cellular expulsion process that rapidly and selectively ejects dying or infected cells from the epithelial layer.
source: Of particular relevance to Shigella and other gastrointestinal pathogens, cell death of IECs is accompanied by a unique cellular expulsion process that rapidly and selectively ejects dying or infected cells from the epithelial layer, thereby potently limiting pathogen invasion into deeper tissue (Fattinger et al., 2021; Knodler et al., 2014; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fattinger et al., 2021; Knodler et al., 2014; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014.

claim: Cellular expulsion of dying or infected IECs potently limits pathogen invasion into deeper tissue.
source: Of particular relevance to Shigella and other gastrointestinal pathogens, cell death of IECs is accompanied by a unique cellular expulsion process that rapidly and selectively ejects dying or infected cells from the epithelial layer, thereby potently limiting pathogen invasion into deeper tissue (Fattinger et al., 2021; Knodler et al., 2014; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fattinger et al., 2021; Knodler et al., 2014; Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014.

claim: Shigella encodes OspC3 to block Caspase-4 inflammasome activation.
source: Shigella encodes multiple effectors to prevent cell death in human cells, including OspC3 to block Caspase-4 inflammasome activation (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021), IpaH7.8 to inhibit Gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis (Luchetti et al., 2021), OspC1 to suppress Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis (Ashida et al., 2020), and OspD3 to block necroptosis (Ashida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021.

claim: Shigella encodes IpaH7.8 to inhibit Gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis.
source: Shigella encodes multiple effectors to prevent cell death in human cells, including OspC3 to block Caspase-4 inflammasome activation (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021), IpaH7.8 to inhibit Gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis (Luchetti et al., 2021), OspC1 to suppress Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis (Ashida et al., 2020), and OspD3 to block necroptosis (Ashida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Luchetti et al., 2021.

claim: Shigella encodes OspC1 to suppress Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis.
source: Shigella encodes multiple effectors to prevent cell death in human cells, including OspC3 to block Caspase-4 inflammasome activation (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021), IpaH7.8 to inhibit Gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis (Luchetti et al., 2021), OspC1 to suppress Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis (Ashida et al., 2020), and OspD3 to block necroptosis (Ashida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashida et al., 2020.

claim: Shigella encodes OspD3 to block necroptosis.
source: Shigella encodes multiple effectors to prevent cell death in human cells, including OspC3 to block Caspase-4 inflammasome activation (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021), IpaH7.8 to inhibit Gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis (Luchetti et al., 2021), OspC1 to suppress Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis (Ashida et al., 2020), and OspD3 to block necroptosis (Ashida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashida et al., 2020.

claim: Mice are resistant to oral Shigella challenge because Shigella is unable to counteract epithelial NAIP–NLRC4-dependent cell death and expulsion.
source: Mice, however, are resistant to oral Shigella challenge because Shigella is unable to counteract epithelial NAIP–NLRC4-dependent cell death and expulsion (Chang et al., 2013; Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2013 and Mitchell et al., 2020.

claim: Removal of the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome renders mice susceptible to shigellosis.
source: Removal of the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome renders mice susceptible to shigellosis, providing a tractable genetic model to dissect Shigella pathogenesis after oral infection in vivo (Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mitchell et al., 2020.

claim: Caspase-11 is a cytosolic sensor of LPS.
source: We find that Caspase-11 (CASP11), a cytosolic sensor of LPS and the mouse ortholog of human Caspase-4 (Shi et al., 2014), provides modest protection from Shigella infection in the absence of NAIP–NLRC4.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2014.

claim: Caspase-11 is the mouse ortholog of human Caspase-4.
source: We find that Caspase-11 (CASP11), a cytosolic sensor of LPS and the mouse ortholog of human Caspase-4 (Shi et al., 2014), provides modest protection from Shigella infection in the absence of NAIP–NLRC4.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2014.

claim: Caspase-11 provides modest protection from Shigella infection in the absence of NAIP–NLRC4.
source: We find that Caspase-11 (CASP11), a cytosolic sensor of LPS and the mouse ortholog of human Caspase-4 (Shi et al., 2014), provides modest protection from Shigella infection in the absence of NAIP–NLRC4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Shigella effector OspC3 antagonizes Caspase-11 activity.
source: However, this protection is limited when Shigella expresses OspC3, an effector that antagonizes Caspase-11 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic removal of ospC3 from Shigella results in a significant CASP11-dependent reduction in bacterial colonization of IECs.
source: As in humans, this pathway is antagonized by the Shigella effector OspC3, and genetic removal of ospC3 from Shigella results in a significant CASP11-dependent reduction in bacterial colonization of IECs and virulence.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic removal of ospC3 from Shigella results in a significant CASP11-dependent reduction in virulence.
source: As in humans, this pathway is antagonized by the Shigella effector OspC3, and genetic removal of ospC3 from Shigella results in a significant CASP11-dependent reduction in bacterial colonization of IECs and virulence.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TNFα defends mouse IECs from bacterial colonization.
source: We also find that TNFα, a cytokine that can induce TNF receptor 1 (TNFRI)-dependent extrinsic apoptosis (Piguet et al., 1998), defends mouse IECs from bacterial colonization and limits subsequent disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TNFα limits disease during Shigella infection.
source: We also find that TNFα, a cytokine that can induce TNF receptor 1 (TNFRI)-dependent extrinsic apoptosis (Piguet et al., 1998), defends mouse IECs from bacterial colonization and limits subsequent disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TNFα can induce TNF receptor 1 (TNFRI)-dependent extrinsic apoptosis.
source: We also find that TNFα, a cytokine that can induce TNF receptor 1 (TNFRI)-dependent extrinsic apoptosis (Piguet et al., 1998), defends mouse IECs from bacterial colonization and limits subsequent disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Piguet et al., 1998.

claim: TNFα-dependent protection is strongest when mice lack both NAIP–NLRC4 and CASP11.
source: TNFα-dependent protection is strongest when mice lack both NAIP–NLRC4 and CASP11, revealing a hierarchical program of cell death pathways that counteract Shigella in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Casp1/11–/–Ripk3–/– mice are largely protected from disease.
source: Casp1/11–/–Ripk3–/– and Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice, which lack some but not all key components of pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis, are largely protected from disease, revealing redundancies among these pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice are largely protected from disease.
source: Casp1/11–/–Ripk3–/– and Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice, which lack some but not all key components of pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis, are largely protected from disease, revealing redundancies among these pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice are hyper-susceptible to shigellosis.
source: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice, however, are hyper-susceptible to shigellosis, indicating that programmed cell death is a predominant host defense mechanism against Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Programmed cell death is a predominant host defense mechanism against Shigella infection.
source: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice, however, are hyper-susceptible to shigellosis, indicating that programmed cell death is a predominant host defense mechanism against Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing hyper-susceptibility in mice lacking multiple cell death pathways.

claim: IL-1R-mediated signaling does not have an apparent effect on Shigella pathogenesis.
source: Furthermore, neither interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R)-mediated signaling nor myeloid-restricted NAIP–NLRC4 have an apparent effect on Shigella pathogenesis, suggesting that it is cell death of IECs that primarily protects mice from shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Myeloid-restricted NAIP–NLRC4 does not have an apparent effect on Shigella pathogenesis.
source: Furthermore, neither interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R)-mediated signaling nor myeloid-restricted NAIP–NLRC4 have an apparent effect on Shigella pathogenesis, suggesting that it is cell death of IECs that primarily protects mice from shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell death of IECs primarily protects mice from shigellosis.
source: Furthermore, neither interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R)-mediated signaling nor myeloid-restricted NAIP–NLRC4 have an apparent effect on Shigella pathogenesis, suggesting that it is cell death of IECs that primarily protects mice from shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of effect of IL-1R and myeloid NAIP-NLRC4.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited only modest weight loss (5–10% of starting weight) through two days and began to recover by day 3.
source: The B6.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited only modest weight loss (5–10% of starting weight) through two days and began to recover by day 3 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice continued to lose weight through day 3 (10–15% of starting weight).
source: The 129.Nlrc4–/– mice, however, continued to lose weight through day 3 (10–15% of starting weight) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IECs from 129.Nlrc4–/– mice harbored >10-fold higher intracellular Shigella burdens than those from B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: IECs from 129.Nlrc4–/– mice harbored >10-fold higher intracellular Shigella burdens than those from B6.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had higher levels of inflammatory cytokines CXCL1 and IL-1β in their intestinal tissue than B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: We also found that 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had higher levels of inflammatory cytokines CXCL1 and IL-1β in their intestinal tissue, as measured by ELISA (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: CXCL1 and IL-1β are NF-κB-induced cytokines previously implicated in driving disease during shigellosis by initiating inflammation and promoting innate immune cell recruitment to the gut.
source: CXCL1 and IL-1β are NF-κB-induced cytokines previously implicated in driving disease during shigellosis by initiating inflammation and promoting innate immune cell recruitment to the gut (Arondel et al., 1999; Sansonetti et al., 1999; Sansonetti et al., 2000; Singer and Sansonetti, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arondel et al., 1999; Sansonetti et al., 1999; Sansonetti et al., 2000; Singer and Sansonetti, 2004.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited significantly more gross cecum shrinkage than B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: The 129.Nlrc4–/– mice also exhibited significantly more gross cecum shrinkage than B6.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 1E) and there were modest but insignificant increases in diarrhea (as measured by the wet weight to dry weight ratio of mouse feces) in 129.Nlrc4–/– mice relative to the B6.Nlrc4–/– mice at 2 and 3 days post-infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: All 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had occult blood in their feces on at least one day (day 2 or 3), with many having occult or macroscopic blood on both days.
source: All 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had occult blood in their feces on at least one of these days, with many having occult or macroscopic blood on both days.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice did not exhibit fecal blood.
source: In contrast, B6.Nlrc4–/– mice did not exhibit fecal blood.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 129 mice are naturally deficient for Caspase-11.
source: Notably, 129 mice are naturally deficient for Caspase-11 (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: F1 B6/129.Nlrc4–/– hybrids were relatively resistant to Shigella challenge and their disease profile more consistently resembled that of the parental B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: We infected these F1 B6/129. Nlrc4–/– hybrids and found that they were relatively resistant to Shigella challenge and their disease profile more consistently resembled that of the parental B6.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F.

claim: Backcrossed Nlrc4–/– mice that were heterozygous B6/129 at Casp11 were more resistant to shigellosis than backcrossed Nlrc4–/– mice that were 129/129 at Casp11.
source: Indeed, backcrossed Nlrc4–/– mice that were heterozygous B6/129 at Casp11 (Figure 1, maroon symbols) were more resistant to shigellosis than backcrossed Nlrc4–/– mice that were 129/129 at Casp11 (Figure 1, dark blue symbols).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice that were heterozygous B6/129 at Casp11 showed a similar weight loss pattern to the parental B6.Nlrc4–/– mice and began to recover by day 3.
source: Mice that were heterozygous B6/129 at Casp11 showed a similar weight loss pattern to the parental B6.Nlrc4–/– mice and began to recover by day 3 while the weight loss in mice that were homozygous 129/129 at Casp11 phenocopied that of the parental 129.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mice that were homozygous 129/129 at Casp11 exhibited significantly enhanced bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium.
source: Consistent with these results, mice that were homozygous 129/129 at Casp11 also exhibited significantly enhanced bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hiccs did not significantly correlate with increased susceptibility to shigellosis.
source: In contrast to Casp11, we found that Hiccs did not significantly correlate with increased susceptibility to shigellosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice experienced a fivefold increase in Shigella burdens in IECs relative to B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11+/– mice.
source: While B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice did not experience more weight loss (Figure 2A), cecum shrinkage (Figure 2B), or diarrhea (Figure 2C) than B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11+/–, there was a fivefold increase in Shigella burdens in IECs from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice (Figure 2D), indicating that Caspase-11 protects the mouse epithelium from bacterial colonization in the absence of NLRC4.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Caspase-11 protects the mouse epithelium from bacterial colonization in the absence of NLRC4.
source: While B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice did not experience more weight loss (Figure 2A), cecum shrinkage (Figure 2B), or diarrhea (Figure 2C) than B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11+/–, there was a fivefold increase in Shigella burdens in IECs from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice (Figure 2D), indicating that Caspase-11 protects the mouse epithelium from bacterial colonization in the absence of NLRC4.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased bacterial burdens in Casp11-deficient mice.

claim: Intestinal tissue from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice expressed significantly higher levels of CXCL1 than tissue from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11+/–.
source: Intestinal tissue from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice also expressed significantly higher levels of CXCL1 than tissue from B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11+/– (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice challenged with ΔospC3 S. flexneri were less susceptible to infection than those challenged with WT S. flexneri.
source: However, B6.Nlrc4–/– mice challenged with ΔospC3 S. flexneri were less susceptible to infection (Figure 3), exhibiting significantly less weight loss (Figure 3B), a >10-fold decrease in IEC colonization (Figure 3C), reduced cecum shrinkage (Figure 3D), and a decrease in CXCL1 (Figure 3F) relative to WT-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice challenged with ΔospC3 S. flexneri exhibited a >10-fold decrease in IEC colonization relative to WT-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: However, B6.Nlrc4–/– mice challenged with ΔospC3 S. flexneri were less susceptible to infection (Figure 3), exhibiting significantly less weight loss (Figure 3B), a >10-fold decrease in IEC colonization (Figure 3C), reduced cecum shrinkage (Figure 3D), and a decrease in CXCL1 (Figure 3F) relative to WT-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with ΔospC3 S. flexneri did not display fecal blood while six of the eleven B6.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with WT Shigella did present with fecal blood.
source: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with ΔospC3 S. flexneri did not display fecal blood while six of the eleven B6.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with WT Shigella did present with fecal blood (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: ΔospC3 Shigella is significantly attenuated in the B6.Nlrc4–/– mouse model of shigellosis.
source: These results indicate that ΔospC3 Shigella is significantly attenuated in our B6.Nlrc4–/– mouse model of shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced disease severity with ΔospC3 Shigella.

claim: Both WT and ΔospC3 Shigella caused severe disease in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice.
source: However, both WT and ΔospC3 Shigella caused severe disease in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice, with comparable weight loss, bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, cecum lengths, diarrhea, and fecal blood (Figure 4A–D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–D and G.

claim: ΔospC3-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited significantly less weight loss, bacterial burdens, cecum shrinkage, and IL-1β relative to ΔospC3-infected B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice.
source: ΔospC3-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited significantly less weight loss, bacterial burdens, cecum shrinkage, and IL-1β relative to ΔospC3-infected B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice (Figure 4A, B, C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, B, C and F.

claim: Caspase-11 is the primary physiological target of OspC3 in vivo.
source: These results indicate that Caspase-11 is the primary physiological target of OspC3 in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the effect of OspC3 deletion is dependent on Caspase-11.

claim: Caspase-11 provides potent defense against Shigella in the absence of OspC3.
source: Caspase-11 provides potent defense against Shigella in the absence of OspC3, although this does not appear sufficient to fully compensate for the loss of NLRC4, as ΔospC3-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibit a phenotype that trends toward modest susceptibility relative to WT-infected WT control mice (Figure 3, Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: OspC3-dependent inhibition of Caspase-11 is required for Shigella virulence.
source: These results confirm prior reports that OspC3 inhibits Caspase-11 in vivo (Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021) and further show that OspC3-dependent inhibition of Caspase-11 is required for Shigella virulence.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Kobayashi et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Mou et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2021.

claim: OspC3-dependent inhibition of Caspase-11 is likely incomplete, as Caspase-11 still provides a small degree of protection in B6.Nlrc4–/– mice even when Shigella expresses OspC3.
source: Nonetheless, this inhibition is likely incomplete, as Caspase-11 still provides a small degree of protection in B6.Nlrc4–/– mice even when Shigella expresses OspC3 (Figures 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: iNlrc4+Lyz2Cre+ mice phenocopied B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: Surprisingly, iNlrc4+Lyz2Cre+ mice phenocopied B6.Nlrc4–/– mice, and did not exhibit significant differences in weight loss, bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, cecum length, or diarrhea (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–E.

claim: Epithelial but not myeloid cell NLRC4 is protective against oral Shigella infection.
source: Unlike iNlrc4+Lyz2Cre+ mice, iNlrc4+VilCreCre+ mice were strongly protected from oral Shigella infection, implying that epithelial but not myeloid cell NLRC4 is protective.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of iNlrc4+Lyz2Cre+ and iNlrc4+VilCreCre+ mice.

claim: NLRC4-dependent pyroptosis in macrophages is neither a major driver of disease pathogenesis nor bacterial colonization in the oral mouse model of infection.
source: We conclude that NLRC4-dependent pyroptosis in macrophages is neither a major driver of disease pathogenesis nor bacterial colonization in our oral mouse model of infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no protective effect of myeloid NLRC4.

claim: Nlrc4–/–Il1r1–/– mice largely phenocopied Nlrc4–/–Il1r1+/– mice.
source: Surprisingly, Nlrc4–/–Il1r1–/– mice largely phenocopied Nlrc4–/–Il1r1+/– mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IL-1 signaling might affect neutrophil recruitment but is not a primary driver of pathogenesis or protection during oral Shigella infection.
source: Overall, these results indicate that, despite the increases in IL-1β consistently seen in susceptible mice, IL-1 signaling might affect neutrophil recruitment but is not a primary driver of pathogenesis or protection during oral Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing modest effects of IL-1R deficiency.

claim: NLRC4-dependent resistance to shigellosis is likely due to the initiation of pyroptosis and expulsion in IECs and not myeloid cell pyroptosis nor IL-1 signaling.
source: NLRC4-dependent resistance to shigellosis is therefore likely due to the initiation of pyroptosis and expulsion in IECs and not myeloid cell pyroptosis nor IL-1 signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of effect of myeloid NLRC4 and IL-1R.

claim: TNFα has been shown to promote Salmonella-induced IEC death and dislodgement.
source: Another cell death initiator in the intestine is TNFα, which has been shown to promote Salmonella-induced IEC death and dislodgement (Fattinger et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fattinger et al., 2021.

claim: TNFα initiates Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis through TNFRI engagement particularly when NF-κB signaling is altered or blocked.
source: TNFα initiates Caspase-8-dependent apoptosis through TNFRI engagement particularly when NF-κB signaling is altered or blocked (Leppkes et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2004; Piguet et al., 1998; Ruder et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leppkes et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2004; Piguet et al., 1998; Ruder et al., 2019.

claim: Shigella encodes several effectors reported to inhibit NF-κB signaling.
source: Shigella encodes several effectors reported to inhibit NF-κB signaling (Ashida et al., 2010; Ashida et al., 2013; de Jong et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2005; Newton et al., 2010; Sanada et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013), and thus, we hypothesized that TNFα might restrict Shigella by inducing death of infected IECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ashida et al., 2010; Ashida et al., 2013; de Jong et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2005; Newton et al., 2010; Sanada et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013.

claim: TNFα neutralization in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice significantly increased susceptibility to Shigella infection.
source: To test this, we repeated the experiment in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice and, indeed, found that TNFα neutralization on this genetic background significantly increased susceptibility to Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice treated with antibody to TNFα experienced an ~5% increase in weight loss, a 10-fold increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, and significant increases in colonic shrinkage, diarrhea, and inflammatory cytokines.
source: Mice treated with antibody to TNFα experienced an ~5% increase in weight loss, a 10-fold increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, and significant increases in colonic shrinkage, diarrhea, and inflammatory cytokines (Figure 7F–H and J–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F–H and J–N.

claim: TNFα levels were elevated significantly in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice, indicating that expression of this cytokine is induced in susceptible mice.
source: TNFα levels were elevated significantly in B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice, indicating that expression of this cytokine is induced in susceptible mice (Figure 7N).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7N.

claim: A hierarchy of cell death pathways (NLRC4>CASP11>TNFα–CASP8) protects the intestinal epithelium from Shigella infection.
source: These results suggest that a hierarchy of cell death pathways protect the intestinal epithelium from Shigella infection. NLRC4 appears to be both necessary and sufficient to protect mice from shigellosis, but in the absence of NLRC4, both Caspase-11 (even in the presence of Shigella effector OspC3) and TNFα can provide modest secondary protection (Figures 1, 2 and 7A–E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of different cell death pathways.

claim: Casp1/11+/–Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice largely phenocopied WT B6 mice and were resistant to infection.
source: We found that Casp1/11+/–Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice largely phenocopied WT B6 mice, and were resistant to infection, exhibiting minimal weight loss, diarrhea, cecal or colonic shrinkage, and no fecal blood (Figure 8A, B, D, E, F, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B, D, E, F, I.

claim: Caspase-8 and RIPK3 are not necessary for resistance to Shigella in the presence of functional NLRC4–CASP1 and CASP11 inflammasomes.
source: These results suggest that Caspase-8 and RIPK3 are not necessary for resistance to Shigella in the presence of functional NLRC4–CASP1 and CASP11 inflammasomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing resistance in Casp8–/–Ripk3–/– mice.

claim: Casp1/11–/–Casp8+/–Ripk3–/– mice were not fully resistant to disease and experienced modest but significant weight loss (~5% relative to WT) and significant increases in cecal and colonic shrinkage.
source: Interestingly, Casp1/11–/–Casp8+/–Ripk3–/– mice were not fully resistant to disease and experienced modest but significant weight loss (~5% relative to WT) and significant increases in cecal and colonic shrinkage (Figure 8B, E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B, E and F.

claim: Caspase-8 is not sufficient to render mice fully resistant to Shigella infection.
source: This result indicates that Caspase-8 is not sufficient to render mice fully resistant to Shigella infection, perhaps because it is antagonized by Shigella effector OspC1, which suppresses Caspase-8 activity in human cell lines (Ashida et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation to Ashida et al., 2020.

claim: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice were highly susceptible to Shigella infection, exhibiting severe weight loss (~15% of starting weight), diarrhea, and cecal and colonic shrinkage.
source: The most striking observation was that Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice were highly susceptible to Shigella infection, exhibiting severe weight loss (~15% of starting weight), diarrhea, and cecal and colonic shrinkage (Figure 8A, B and D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B and D–F.

claim: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice exhibited a massive (>500×) increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium.
source: These mice also exhibited a massive (>500×) increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium (Figure 8C) and elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: All Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice presented with blood in their feces.
source: All Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice presented with blood in their feces (Figure 8I) and one of the ten mice also died of shigellosis within 2 days of infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: One of the ten Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice died of shigellosis within 2 days of infection.
source: All Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice presented with blood in their feces (Figure 8I) and one of the ten mice also died of shigellosis within 2 days of infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Redundant cell death pathways protect mice from disease upon oral Shigella challenge.
source: Taken together, our results imply that redundant cell death pathways protect mice from disease upon oral Shigella challenge.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing protection with some but not all cell death pathways removed.

claim: Genetic removal of three caspases essential to the cell death response leads to severe shigellosis.
source: Genetic removal of three caspases essential to this response leads to severe shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing severe disease in Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice.

claim: Removal of one or two caspases critical to the cell death response does not lead to severe disease because of significant compensation from the other pathway(s).
source: However, removal of one or two caspases critical to this response does not lead to severe disease because of significant compensation from the other pathway(s).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing protection in mice lacking some but not all cell death pathways.

claim: The hierarchy of cell death pathways may be established by the order in which a pathway can sense invasive Shigella within the epithelium and initiate a cell death response.
source: We speculate that this hierarchy may be established by the order in which a pathway can sense invasive Shigella within the epithelium and initiate a cell death response.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: OspC3 has been shown to be required for virulence during intraperitoneal mouse infection by S. flexneri.
source: While OspC3 has been shown to be required for virulence during intraperitoneal mouse infection by S. flexneri (Li et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2021) and for intestinal colonization by S. sonnei in WT mice (Alphonse et al., 2022), the role of this effector has not been studied in an oral mouse model of infection where Shigella invades and replicates within the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Oh et al., 2021.

claim: OspC3 has been shown to be required for intestinal colonization by S. sonnei in WT mice.
source: While OspC3 has been shown to be required for virulence during intraperitoneal mouse infection by S. flexneri (Li et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2021) and for intestinal colonization by S. sonnei in WT mice (Alphonse et al., 2022), the role of this effector has not been studied in an oral mouse model of infection where Shigella invades and replicates within the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alphonse et al., 2022.

claim: TNFα is a major driver of pathology during Crohn's disease.
source: For example, TNFα is a major driver of pathology during Crohn's disease (van Dullemen et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Dullemen et al., 1995.

claim: In the context of Salmonella infection, TNFα appears to drive widespread pathological death and dislodgement of IECs at 72 hr post-infection.
source: In the context of Salmonella infection, TNFα appears to drive widespread pathological death and dislodgement of IECs at 72 hr post-infection (Fattinger et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fattinger et al., 2021.

claim: TNFα is protective during oral Shigella infection.
source: Here, we show that TNFα is protective during oral Shigella infection, providing a rationale for why this cytokine is produced in the intestine.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– and 129.Nlrc4–/– mice, TNFα neutralization led to a striking increase in severity of infection and a 10-fold increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium.
source: In both B6.Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– and 129.Nlrc4–/– mice, TNFα neutralization led to a striking increase in severity of infection and a 10-fold increase in bacterial colonization of the intestinal epithelium (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TNFα promotes epithelial defense by initiating IEC apoptosis of infected cells in which NF-κB signaling is blocked.
source: Given the redundant, overlapping functions of both Caspase-11 and TNFα in the absence of NLRC4, we favor the hypothesis that TNFα promotes epithelial defense by initiating IEC apoptosis of infected cells in which NF-κB signaling is blocked (Ashida et al., 2010; Ashida et al., 2013; de Jong et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2005; Newton et al., 2010; Sanada et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice experienced more severe disease and epithelial colonization than Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice.
source: Although we did not directly compare the two mouse strains, Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice (Figure 8) experienced more severe disease and epithelial colonization than Nlrc4–/–Casp11–/– mice (Figures 2, 4 and 7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of data across different figures.

claim: The additional susceptibility of Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice results from the absence of TNFRI–CASP8-dependent apoptosis and possibly from the absence of RIPK3-dependent necroptosis.
source: We speculate that the additional susceptibility of Casp1/11/8–/–Ripk3–/– mice results from the absence of TNFRI–CASP8-dependent apoptosis and possibly from the absence of RIPK3-dependent necroptosis.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: The critical protective role of Caspase-8 in the absence of Caspase-1, Caspase-11, and RIPK3 suggests that this cell death initiator is not strongly antagonized by OspC1 in mice.
source: While both apoptosis and necroptosis appear to be blocked in human cells by Shigella effectors OspC1 and OspD3, respectively (Ashida et al., 2020), the critical protective role of Caspase-8 in the absence of Caspase-1, Caspase-11, and RIPK3 suggests that this cell death initiator is not strongly antagonized by OspC1 in mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation to Ashida et al., 2020.

claim: CASP8 might contribute to defense against Shigella via a mechanism that is independent of TNFα or NLRC4-dependent cell death.
source: In addition, we note that CASP8 is a pleiotropic enzyme and might contribute to defense against Shigella via a mechanism that is independent of TNFα or NLRC4-dependent cell death (Gitlin et al., 2020; Philip et al., 2016; Schwarzer et al., 2020; Stolzer et al., 2022; Weng et al., 2014; Woznicki et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Gitlin et al., 2020; Philip et al., 2016; Schwarzer et al., 2020; Stolzer et al., 2022; Weng et al., 2014; Woznicki et al., 2021.

claim: The commonly held belief is that macrophage pyroptosis and IL-1 signaling drive Shigella pathogenesis.
source: Despite the commonly held belief that macrophage pyroptosis and IL-1 signaling drive Shigella pathogenesis (Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019; Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008), we find no major protective or pathogenic role for either during Shigella infection (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is presented as an established belief in the field, supported by citations to Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019 and Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008.

claim: Epithelial-specific cell death and expulsion may be the key mechanism that protects mice from Shigella.
source: These data suggest that epithelial-specific cell death and expulsion may be the key mechanism that protects mice from Shigella.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of effect of myeloid NLRC4 and IL-1R.

claim: There is a correlation between bacterial burdens in IECs and pathogenicity in the experiments.
source: We observed a correlation between bacterial burdens in IECs and pathogenicity in our experiments, indicating that the extent to which Shigella can colonize the intestinal epithelium dictates the severity of disease during infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The extent to which Shigella can colonize the intestinal epithelium dictates the severity of disease during infection.
source: We observed a correlation between bacterial burdens in IECs and pathogenicity in our experiments, indicating that the extent to which Shigella can colonize the intestinal epithelium dictates the severity of disease during infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed correlation between bacterial burdens and disease severity.
